utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Reidy, you're continuing with examination-in-chief. Yes, Ms. Baen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Just for purposes of the record, Your Honour, our client has waived his appearance today and will watch the trial via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Also, yesterday afternoon, the Prosecutors asked if my client would waive any issues regarding his identification by this witness. I discussed it through an interpreter with my client, and we have faxed over a written waiver where he says he's willing to waive that so we don't delay the trial. I'm having that faxed back into the Registry just so that it's in the record so that there's no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Reidy, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Delic.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yesterday I began to ask you some questions about the conditions for you living in Bosanski Samac, between the 22nd of April and the 4th of September, 1992, and I'd like to pick up on that topic again this afternoon. Could you please tell me, during that time after your husband was arrested until the time you left Bosanski Samac, did you continue to have electricity in your home all the time?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the time. Because that part of town was cut off from electrical supply because of shelling or whatever. At any rate, starting with mid-June, we had no more power. What was particularly curious to me was that non-Serbs did not have telephone communication already in the month of May. Their telephone lines were down for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So for clarification, the electricity from mid-June, was that cut off for everyone, or did you notice that some people had electricity and others had no electricity?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my part of town, people had no electricity for the most part, all those who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the telephone lines, you said that non-Serbs did not have telephone communication already in the month of May. Do I understand you to say that at the beginning, in April, that you were able to use your telephones, but that at some stage you lost the telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. In the beginning, the telephone communication functioned. But at the later stage, we were cut off, while our Serbian, Serb neighbours, still had telephone communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have an explanation how she got to know that the Serbian neighbours had communication. And also on the electricity, at the part of town where she used to live, was this a mixed neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'll pursue those two clarifications right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The first one perhaps is on the matter of the electricity. Was the area where you used to live in town, was that a mixed neighbourhood, and so was it that both Serb apartments and Muslim and Croat apartments all suffered from the same extent to lack of electricity?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as electricity is concerned, I can't say that non-Serb population was targeted. That part of town had a mixed population. All ethnic groups were represented. And I can't say that I did not have electricity because I was not a Serb. But with regard to telephone communications, the case was clearer. For instance, my left-hand and my right-hand neighbours, next-door neighbours, were Serb families, and I know for sure that their telephones continued working.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Then you say "for sure." I mean, what does that mean? Your left-hand and your right-hand neighbour, did you try to call them yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't call them. But we shared gardens and open fences, so I could communicate with them. I could talk to them. And they would tell me that they had called their family and relatives in Samac and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that you got cut off. Are you speaking specifically about your apartment, or do you know of other non-Serb families who also lost the ability to use the telephones?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that other citizens who continued living in the town and were not Serbs did not have the possibility to communicate by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the reason you know this for certain is what?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from conversations I had with those persons, and they told me that they could not telephone anyone either inside the town or outside of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy. I wonder whether you could clarify with the witness whether once it was known, for example, that her family's telephone was cut off, whether she communicated with any administrative person in Bosanski Samac to see whether -- what the problem was and whether the phone could be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you understand Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not approach or address anyone because fear already reigned to such an extent that it never occurred to me even to ask for an official explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of your other non-Serb -- the non-Serb people you'd spoken to who had also lost their telephone lines, do you know if they had ever inquired why the telephone lines were no longer working or if something could be done about it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that I knew did not do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just two quick clarifications. How long were you without electricity, and how long were you without the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking for the exact date when our telephone stopped working, I couldn't tell you. But I know it was sometime in the middle of May. Starting with mid-May, I no longer had telephone access. And electricity was cut off in the end of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, you also mentioned yesterday that a curfew was imposed at the beginning of the takeover. Did that curfew continue throughout the time you stayed in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time I stayed in Bosanski Samac, the curfew was on. And it lasted from 9.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m. In the summer season, it was shifted to 10.00 p.m. and lasted until 6.00 a.m. Windows had to be shaded and there was a ban on movement in that interval.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague has just brought to my attention an omission on the transcript which could become important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And it was the question posed by Your Honour Judge Singh, which was, I believe, did you ever get back the electricity and the telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the witness said, "No." But the question is not recorded. So maybe now the record could reflect that was Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: If it was restored, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, that was just a problem with the record. This curfew, did you know whether all citizens obeyed the curfew? Or was there a problem with respect to Serbs and non-Serbs with respect to obeying the curfew?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discrimination existed in that respect as well. My Serbian neighbours could move around that as they pleased, and they paid no attention to such rules or bans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I wonder whether you could clarify whether this curfew was imposed on everybody: Serbs, Muslims, Croats, or whether it was just imposed on non-Serbs. And therefore, if it was imposed on everybody, that some chose to disobey it. I'd just like to get a better sense of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you -- Ms. Delic, could you clarify when the curfew was announced, was it directed to the entire population, or was it specifically directed at certain groups of the population?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, non-Serbian population did not dare to violate the curfew. I don't know whether the others were allowed to disregard it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just one supplementary question, Ms. Reidy. I wonder whether you could clarify with the witness how the population of Bosanski Samac knew that there was a curfew. How was it proclaimed: posters, word of mouth, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, could you tell us how the curfew was imposed. And perhaps you could tell us the first time you heard about it, which I believe you testified yesterday, and whether there was further information about the curfew given to the population.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was announced on the radio, the Serbian radio of Bosanski Samac, which made such announcements and announced such decisions, and this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And in the announcement -- the announcement was directed at the population as a whole, or at certain groups of the population?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the way this announcement was formulated, I understood it only concerned non-Serbian population. I cannot remember right now whether it was expressly said that Serbs could move around during the curfew. But I remember that non-Serbs had an obligation to adhere to the curfew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I apologise, Ms. Reidy. But just an extra supplementary question. This was an announcement on the radio. When the announcer on the radio made this announcement, was it stated who had issued this proclamation? Was it the Crisis Staff? Was it some other body? Was it in the name of an individual or individuals representing that body? I think that would be important for us to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, could you please answer that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was behind both these announcements, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do forgive me. When you say, "The Crisis Staff was behind these announcements," did the radio broadcast mention the Crisis Staff to your hearing? Because you probably heard the radio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And was the Crisis Staff mentioned in the radio broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was mentioned in the announcement as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Reidy, so that the witness is quicker, when you're talking about various discriminatory measures, please make your question very specific and try to get to identify the source, whether she's relating from her observation, from documents, from the radio, television, so that we all quickly -- I mean clear, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'll adopt that approach in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, could I also ask a clarification before we move on from this? You did say that the Crisis Staff was behind both announcements. Could you clarify when you're talking about both announcements which announcements you mean, as that implies there was at least -- well, there was two announcements.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the announcement that was made on the radio, but also in the form of posters put up in various public places around town. And one of the provisions in such announcements said that it was prohibited for two or more non-Serbs to gather in public or socialise, and this decision was also signed by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So can I be clear. The announcement -- or you learned about the curfew through a radio announcement which specifically said that the Crisis Staff imposed this curfew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever see posters or notices, as you said, in public places with the similar information just about the curfew, or was your source of information about the curfew the radio, the Serbian radio?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only found out from the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So Ms. Reidy, the witness has said that these posters were signed by the Crisis Staff. If she only heard this information on the radio, how does she know the posters were signed by the Crisis Staff? And secondly, if signed by the Crisis Staff, who in the Crisis Staff signed it?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just hoping to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you spoke of posters you saw in town. The posters you saw in town, did they relate, then, to the curfew, or did they relate to other measures which were imposed on you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems I should clarify a bit more. I was talking about the decision to impose the curfew, which was announced on the radio, and it was said in the announcement that this was a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac. Other decisions were published in the form of posters which were put up in various public places around town: the doors of shops and such places. At the bottom of such posters, it also said that the decision was made by the Crisis Staff, and the signature below was that of Blagoje Simic, the chairman.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one of those posters you said you saw related to a prohibition on two or more Serbs to gather in public places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy, I do have to refer you back to page 9, your question, line 15, where you asked the question re: the curfew, "Was your source of information about the curfew the radio, the Serbian radio?" Answer from the witness: "I only found out from the ^^^ radio." Hence my question is: How does the witness know about the posters and whatever is on it if she only knew about the radio and didn't see the posters? Your question to her was then on line 13, and you say "Now, one of those posters you said you saw," but the witness says she only found out from the radio. So this is rather confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I have to say my interpretation of the transcript was that it was clear that the witness had said the information about the curfew was from the radio and then she'd said she had seen other posters in town but they don't relate to the curfew but to other decisions but -- it's now gone off my screen. I can go over this evidence if -- I don't want there to be confusion on the record, because that certainly my understanding of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think it says that other decisions were in the form of posters. And then she went on to say that in the name of the Crisis Staff and the name of Blagoje Simic appears. But she -- as I said earlier to you, the source of the information, she doesn't say that she saw that herself. It's important that if she sees something, she tells us; she hears something of her own personal knowledge, she tells us. If "X" said something, she says "X" said something. You follow? We don't want gossip and rumours to come up in evidence here. Please try to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I'm trying to avoid that. I will, I think maybe just for clarification for the record I'll -- I hope I'll not going to get into repetition, I'll just go over these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, could I ask you just to return again just to the information concerning the imposition of the curfew. Did you hear that through the radio, Radio Serbian Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you hear that -- you heard that yourself. You didn't hear it from someone. You heard the actual radio announcement yourself?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I heard it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you heard that announcement yourself, you heard it being said on the announcement that the curfew was being imposed on the authority or instruction of the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At that time, with that announcement, did you hear any specific name being mentioned from the Crisis Staff, or was it just generally the authority of the Crisis Staff that was being invoked?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. The information about the curfew, did you see it repeated anywhere else, on a poster, a notice, a sign -- a letter brought to your door, or was your sole source of information what you yourself heard on the radio?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, as I said, I heard it on the radio. There were no pamphlets or any other things. I just heard it on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any other stage, did you again see the same information from another source on a poster or on a notice, just about the curfew, or was your personal knowledge of the curfew based on the radio announcement?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you clarify that -- okay. I'm going to ask you, at any other stage did you see that information on written form on a poster or a notice -- just about the imposition of the curfew.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw it in any other written form.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So it remains that your personal knowledge of the curfew was based on the radio announcement?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you said you also learnt of an order that there wasn't to be a gathering together of, I think you said, two or more non-Serbs. How did you learn of that information?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that by reading about it on a notice or a poster that was posted on several public places around the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you saw this instruction yourself, that there were to be -- not to be a gathering of two or more non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you saw that poster, could you see who was giving that order? Could you see a name or a signature or a stamp? And if you could, could you, to the best of your memory, tell us what you saw on that stamp -- you saw on the poster.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was in the place where the signature was supposed to be. It was the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac. It was stamped. The stamp had the 4-S sign in the middle. And around the edge of the stamp, it said: "Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac." The poster was also signed by Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give an idea of the time when it was that you first saw a poster like this.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The posters appeared a little later, perhaps only in the month of June. I can't tell you the exact date when the poster first appeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see other posters like the one you've just spoken about, that had other information or instructions about what was permitted and what wasn't permitted?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any other information that was officially announced.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. This prohibition on the gathering of two or more Serbs, can you remember exactly what it meant, what it said you could and couldn't do, and what would happen if there was a gathering of two or more non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I think for the sake of the record, we should have it corrected. Your first statement, Ms. Reidy, was this prohibition on the gathering of two or more Serbs, which you might want to correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would, for the record, like to correct my statement. It was the prohibition on the gathering of two or more non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, if you could explain exactly the nature of that prohibition, and if there was any penalty for violating it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No fines were mentioned, in case of any kind of violation, no penalties. There were no instructions either on how to follow all of these directives.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So the posters simply said that there was to be no gathering of two or more non-Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, did you ever receive an instruction that as a member of the non-Serb community, that you should leave the doors of your apartment unlocked?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received instructions like that, yes. And they were given verbally. This happened during the first few days, when certain military officials also appeared whose duty it was to collect weapons from the citizens and to hand them over. And on that occasion, they emphasised that the doors have to remain unlocked and accessible for any kind of controls or inspections.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So these verbal instructions came from military personnel, to keep your doors open?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But right now I cannot name any persons. But in any case, the person who came that morning was entrusted with making sure that all the weapons were collected from the population, from the citizens in that street, the non-Serbian population, and also to inform and instruct these people about how they should behave in relation to access to their apartments or houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the Serb population instructed to leave their apartment doors unlocked? For example, were your -- did your Serb neighbours keep their apartment doors unlocked?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, and I didn't ask them. We didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you keep your apartment door, as a rule, unlocked throughout your stay in Bosanski Samac until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were unlocked constantly, and they stayed unlocked when we left Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Why did you continue to keep your apartment door unlocked even though you got the instructions in the first few days?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These occasional visits and inspections could take place at any time. I was by myself in the house with the children, so I didn't want to draw attention to myself by violating any of these instructions, so I complied with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of your non-Serb neighbours also did as you did and left their apartment doors unlocked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think you already asked that question. Line 14, page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that was relating to the Serb population. This one was whether she herself personally chose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This question isn't about your Serb neighbours but about other non-Serb persons living in your neighbourhood. Do you know whether they also left their doors locked or whether they chose to lock them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they also kept their doors unlocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you know this from personally seeing their doors unlocked or from conversations with them?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From conversations with them and from the house where I was living in. There was a family living on the ground floor, and I know for sure that they constantly kept their doors unlocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Is my understanding right, then, that when you went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to sleep at night with your children, your door remained unlocked or open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, just as a follow-up to that, did you keep your door unlocked at night because you believed that these inspections or checks you talked about could happen at any time of the day or night?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was something you could expect. Until that moment, I never expected any such visits. But from that moment on, it was reality, and I kept my doors unlocked in case of any inspection.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know or were you told of any visits which did occur, for example, in the evening or at nights where people would come and inspect or search or check apartments?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, and I know about them. But at this moment, I can't really say specifically who it was and what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But you had sufficient information at that time to want to keep your door unlocked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, you've told us that your husband was arrested on the 22nd of April. Were any attempts made to arrest you before you left Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such attempts. For example, for a period, my husband was in Bosanski Samac from the 22nd of April until the 29th of April. Then he was moved to Brcko, then to Bijeljina. And then on the 13th of May, he was returned to Samac. I remember that date because at that time, during those days, there was a raid that was carried out in order to gather all the Croat women in town, to round up all the Croat women in town. This raid began on the so-called market, on the square where vegetables and fruit were sold and where, in the morning, there would always be a large number of women. One of my neighbours, a Muslim woman, and my -- and my sister-in-law were running from the direction of the market, and they came to my house and told me that I should leave the house as soon as possible because they were going to find me, they would find me. Of course at that moment, I couldn't have known that they were looking specifically for me. But I did take that seriously, and I went to a different apartment with my children in order to be in a more secure place.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you some more questions about this incident. You say it took place on the 13th of May. You were at home at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at home. I'm not sure whether it was exactly the 13th of May or the 12th of May. I really couldn't confirm it right now. But in any case, it was during those two or three days in the middle of May that this was happening. Later, I would find out that as a Croat woman, I was also on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come to that in a minute. But just for the time being, I'd like us to make sure this incident at the market place is clear for the record. You were at home, and I understand that your neighbour and your sister-in-law came to your house, having left the marketplace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And they told you what had happened to them in the marketplace just moments before they ran to your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me what was going on at the market. I must note that both of these women were of Muslim ethnicity, so they were not the ones who were being sought in that raid. So they were able to come to me in a calm manner and help me and tell me that I should leave my house in order to hide.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And what -- you said it was because they were Muslim. What exactly did they tell you? They told you that Croat women were being detained? And if so, by whom and in what manner? Was there some trucks there? Were there military people? Were there police? How much detail did they give you about the manner of the arrests that they had witnessed at the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that there was a truck covered with tarpaulin on the street marked next to the market, and they were simply taking away these women. They recognised these Croat women who were their neighbours and that they were taking them away in this truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, you might be going to do this, but just in case, could you get a clarification from the witness why was it Croat women and not Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, we can deal with that question first. Were you told why there was -- why it was Croat women and not Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't understand why it was just Croat women. Was it in order to meet some quotas or something like that, number of persons. But I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say "to meet some quotas," what did you have in mind, that there was a quota of Croats that should be detained, or what did you mean when you used the term "quota"?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm speaking about. There had already been situations where Croat men were taken away to camps, to isolation camps, in order to be exchanged, so that perhaps the women at that point in time were also being rounded up because of the same reasons. Later it would turn out that a large number of non-Serb population would be taken from their homes and then later exchanged or expelled from the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, you said that there had already been situations where Croat men were taken away to camps, to isolation camps, in order to be exchanged. Do you have personal knowledge of Croat men being detained and being kept in isolation somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the gym of the secondary school, there was a large number of Croats, a large group of Croats, who were in that camp. And it was called an isolation camp. And that it was their fate to be expelled in a number of exchanges. Let me tell you how I know this. I want to emphasise that I was called as a former teacher of that school to tell the new management of that school and my colleagues who were still active at that time, and also that I should hand them over the documents that I had from my students, their birth certificates, their old grade certificates, and other documents like that. In order to enter the school building, I had to pass through the schoolyard, then I went into the school through the back entrance through the yard, and then in the hall -- I looked down the corridor which was leading to the gym -- so through that corridor, you could access a certain number of classrooms. And then it went -- continued on to the gym. So at the entrance to that corridor, there was a soldier standing, and he had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, this -- I'd just like to clarify this incident. You personally received an instruction to go to the school, to help resolve a matter with the new management of the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the school year was about to end, so I found only my Serb colleagues in the staffroom. The new person in town was a well-known teacher, Zarko Milanovic, and there were also some other colleagues there of Serb ethnicity. And they told me that they had to write the graduate certificates for that year. And they asked me in case I still had some documents like that, that I needed to hand them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, could you clarify, then, because I -- I don't think we've heard this before. From what the witness is saying, the secondary school was still continuing to operate as a school, although in the gym there were guards and allegedly the persons who were being detained, mostly of Croat or Muslim ethnicity. But the school was still operating as a school? There was still the faculty common room and teachers and management and graduation certificates. Could you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, could you explain? Was there -- you went to the school by -- let me just take this in -- how did you know that you should go to the school? How were you informed to attend?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A student of mine. She was already in her final class. They sent her to inform me that I should come to the school and to bring with me documents, if I happened to have any at home, the documents that I still had with me from my former students, and also to take out from the locker in my school and hand over those documents as well. So after that visit, I went to school, and I saw what I just explained that I saw. However, there were no pupils, no students in the school. It was just the administrative part, where in the staffroom, which happened to be on the first floor of the school, there were several of my colleagues. They were writing graduation certificates. And in that way, they were finishing the paperwork at the end of the school year.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What month was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the end of May. Because the graduate students already were supposed to finish their school year, so in any kind of emergency circumstances, the school year could be ended in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So when you went to the school, you saw people only carrying out administrative functions but no classes or normal school life going on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the persons carrying out the administrative functions, those you knew, were they all of Serb ethnicity, or were there a mix of ethnicities working at the school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Serbs only. And even the students who helped out were only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You also testified that when you went up there, you saw a soldier guarding the entrance to the secondary school gym; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you ask him who was being held in the secondary school gym or if people were being held in the secondary school gym?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the soldier is concerned, I didn't ask him anything. But upstairs in the staffroom, I ran across a colleague of Serbian ethnicity who taught literature and who was married to a Croat. She herself was a Serb. And at that moment, I found it very unusual -- I found it very unusual to hear from her that she was going to take a mattress down for her husband to use in that isolation room, in confinement. But that's what she said.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So she told you that her husband, who was a Croat, was being detained in isolation in the secondary school gym; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This event you've testified took place at the end of May, and you testified that the event in the marketplace, the attempted arrest of Croat woman took place in the end of May. So by mid-May, when this attempted arrest in the marketplace went on, did you then also have some information that the Croat men had been detained?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Croats were being detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And that was information you heard how, through conversations that people were having, or did you witness anything?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I should mention one example which comes to mind. My brother, also a Croat, was being targeted. And at that moment, he was not in Samac because he tried to stay away, knowing that he was on one of those lists as a Croat. So they came looking for him in my apartment, and they said, "Where is that Ustasha? Is he hiding anywhere here?"

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you had a visit from the police or military persons looking for your brother because he was a Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it police or military who came looking for him? Can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You say he was being targeted. By "targeted," do you mean people were looking for him?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were looking for him by name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that you know he was on -- or he knew he was on one of those lists. Are these lists that you saw or that he saw or people had heard about lists being drawn up? Could you explain what those lists were and if you have any personal knowledge of those lists.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, but I know that this one policeman who came was looking for him specifically and mentioned him by name, although he didn't even know at the time whether my brother was in town or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever see any list with your name or your brother's name on it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with my own eyes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did someone else see a list and tell you that your name was on it?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for a list, including my name, I know for certain that it existed. But the raid which was carried out to round up the people on that list happened a bit later, sometime in mid-September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think that question was unnecessary, because she said earlier that she wouldn't have known if they were looking for her.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That's fine then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Have you said that, Ms. Reidy, though, being that the question was asked and the answer does say -- the witness says, concerning the list, page 245, lines 1, and 2, "As for a list, including my name, I know for certain that it existed." So can we find out how the witness, even if she didn't see the list, how she knew for certain that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, you've testified that you did know a list existed. And I understand from your testimony that the list --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- that list was connected later to a raid in September. But for now, could you please tell the Court how you know that this list existed.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that such a list existed because one of the policemen who were in charge informed me that I was on the list, although I didn't see it with my own eyes. But I know from his words that I was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that at some stage in September, a police officer told you that you were on the list which he was looking for people on, he was searching for people on that list?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to return now to this first incident in the marketplace. I believe you testified that what your sister and your -- your sister-in-law and your Muslim neighbour told you was that there were people in the marketplace taking women that they identified as Croats into trucks. Did they tell you whether this was, again, by the military, or was it by police officers? Did they know, or did they tell you that information?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that the men beside the truck were police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And they told you that they were picking up these Croat women and putting them onto the trucks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you learn where the women on the trucks were taken to?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group of women were taken in the direction of the Crkvina, where they were housed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how do you know that the women were housed in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourteen days later, some of those women -- in fact, at least one of these women whom I knew told me that she had been released to go home, together with her daughter. Nobody explained to her why she was being released or why she had been taken away in the first place, but in any case, she was allowed to go home together with her daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you personally spoke with one of the women who had been detained in the marketplace and taken to Crkvina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The woman is Marija Adriani.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that she said she had been released to go home together with her daughter. Do you know how old her daughter was, and is it a correct understanding that her daughter was detained with her in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daughter was taken away together with her because they found them together in their home, and the daughter was 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So this lady, Mrs. Adriani, she was taken from her house but not from the marketplace that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did she say that other women kept with her in Crkvina had been arrested in the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases in that group. And among those women, were also some who lived in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did she say roughly how many women were detained in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. She seems to have said that they were divided into several rooms. But I don't know exactly how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know which building they were detained in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did she mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Sorry. Perhaps you can tell us how many women did she see at the secondary school going away in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Do you mean away from the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No, no. She went to school. Remember? And then she saw this truck. There were women going into the truck. How many did she see?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, did you see women getting into a truck when you were at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there must be a mistake here somewhere, because we're talking about two different events. First, I discussed the isolation of Croats in the building of the secondary school, and then we continued to discuss the raid which happened later. But these two events are not interrelated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to know, coming back to the earlier point, if you saw how many women were taken into the trucks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know -- were you told how many trucks there were in the marketplace? Was there one truck, or was there more than one truck?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one truck at that moment, on the marketplace. Whether there were any other trucks rounding up people from their homes or other places -- but on the marketplace, there was only one truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And this is the information that your Muslim neighbour and your sister-in-law came to tell you by way of warning not to go to the marketplace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask, in the place where the person you spoke to was detained in Crkvina, did she mention whether or not there were any children detained along with the women, or whether those women who were detained had to abandon their children at home?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That woman was together with her daughter at the time, and those who had children with them at the moment, were taken away together with their children. So there were children in that group, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that the woman you spoke to -- I believe your testimony was that she was released after about 14 days. Do you know if everybody was released after 14 days or she personally only spent 14 days detained in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rather a large number of women was released after a while, and I know another lady, an elderly lady, who was allowed to return to her apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "an elderly lady," can you give us an estimation of how old elderly is? Was she over 65, or ...?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really say she was elderly. It must be a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. And just so -- the other lady who was allowed to return to her apartment, had she been detained by herself, or had she been detained with her children, or indeed did this other lady have any children?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask now about the situation of forced labour or any work obligations that you were asked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, before going on to that, we've heard that these women of Croatian ethnicity and those with children, the children also, were detained in Crkvina. Does the witness have any knowledge from these conversations with the people she knew who returned what the conditions were like in which they were detained and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Delic, I think you've understood what Her Honour Judge Williams has said. So if you have any knowledge about the conditions of the detention and who was in charge of the women while they were being detained, could you please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were not good. The rooms where they were placed had bare floors. And I know they had to hand over any gold jewellery they had, any valuables. But I have no other information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You say that they had bare floors. Do you know if they were given mattresses to sleep on, or did they have to sleep on those bare floors?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't get anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you given any information about if they were given food and water during their detention time?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you given any information about the guards, whether they were police or military personnel, whether they were local people or people that they didn't recognise?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I began to ask you about forced labour. Did you yourself have to perform any forced labour?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you given any reason why you didn't do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No particular explanation was given, but I do know that the first group of women who had to go to work included women who had no small children and who were relatively free of obligations. They either had grown-up children who lived alone, or they were elderly and lived alone again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. As we stated earlier, I think it's not permissible to ask any witness here about the notions and categories which are practically based on the legal -- legal theory and doctrine, which means in particular situation, I think the Prosecutor should refrain to ask this and all other witnesses with these kind of formulations. Maybe the proper way would be -- whether it's a work obligation or something, but forced labour, deportation, prosecution, and all that kind of stuff are, I think, directly -- directly suggestive to witnesses. And finally, they don't know the difference between the various form, for example, in this particular case, of work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. I'm sure Ms. Reidy -- I must apologise to interpreters. I always forget to wait for the interpretation to be completed. You understand what Mr. Pantelic is trying to say about these terms which we are using, "forced labour."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take that point aboard. However, I would also rather not use "work obligation," because obviously that again is debated. That's what the Defence claim. So I'll try to use a neutral term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Neutral language: "Did anybody ask you to work anywhere?" She has already said she was a teacher. Come 17th, she couldn't go. And from the evidence so far, she hasn't gone back to teaching. So you can ask along those neutral lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, as Her Honour Judge Mumba has pointed out, you stopped working as a teacher. Did anyone come to your house and require you to do any other -- either continue as a teacher or to perform any other form of work whilst -- after the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not all the way up to the 27th of June that same year. Until that date, nobody called me up or informed me about anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Prior to the 27th of June, did any of your non-Serb neighbours or relatives have to go perform labour which they had been requested to do or been instructed to do?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that others went out to perform that sort of labour. And I know about women who used to work as saleswomen or clerks in various offices. But during those days, they were picked up early in the morning, loaded onto trucks, and taken out to fields, where they had to do fieldwork.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, when you say "they were picked up early in the morning," are you referring to -- who do you mean by "they" exactly? Which? Serbs? Non-Serbs? Women? Men? A whole mixture? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I was talking about non-Serb women who were called up to perform work obligation of this kind, and they were told at what time to show up at a certain assembly point, from which they were transported by truck to the place where they were supposed to carry out Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you see people -- see these non-Serb women being picked up by the truck, or did someone tell you about the truck picking up these non-Serb women?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One time I saw such a group of women myself, and I recognised [redacted] among the women who were already on the truck waiting to depart.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned also that you knew about women who used to work as saleswomen or clerks. But then in those days, they used to be taken out to the fields. Do I understand you to mean that there was two different types as work, one as salespeople and clerks and one in the fields, or that in the beginning, people worked in the fields and later they worked as clerks? Could you clarify what you mean when you talk about those two different types of labour.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must emphasise that in that period, when those new Serb authorities were coming into being, the women and children from Serb families were not in town at all, were not in their homes. They had been moved for their own safety. The new authorities tried to organise life in town and to bring it back to normal, to organise the work of shop and the exchange of currency. And when I mentioned one of -- some of those women who were taken away to do labour, Suada Hadzialiagic and others -- the new authorities, after a while, managed to normalise life and Serb women and children returned. But the people I mentioned before were out of jobs now, and the women who I mentioned before who worked in those shops earlier were replaced now by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I could pick up this subject at quarter past, since it's now time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just before we adjourn, perhaps you can just tell us what the age of your two children was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My son was born in 1974. He was then aged seven. And my daughter was born in 1981, and she was then aged ten.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The son was born in 1984, '84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And do you think that that could possibly be one reason why you were not detained, you were just left to look after your children at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about the reason why I was not arrested. But as far as the work obligation is concerned, I believe that is the reason why I was spared. Why I was not included in the group of women who were obliged to go out to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall take a break until 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. You are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And before you do, Ms. Reidy, I wonder whether you could seek from the witness whether she has any knowledge concerning her visit to the secondary school when the management and teachers were in the teacher's common room and they were doing things, including issuing graduation certificates. Does she have any knowledge as to whether those graduation certificates were being issued to graduating pupils of all ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mrs. Delic. I think you've heard the question that Judge Williams is interested in. If you have the sort of knowledge that she's interested in, could you please advise the Bench?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't informed about who was issued with the graduation certificates and who later received these graduation certificates. I didn't take part in these talks. Nobody asked me anything about it or informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were your -- did you know any non-Serb students who had been attending the school -- attending the school up until the 17th of April who received a graduation or a -- a graduation certificate?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't have any more contact with the students.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Prior to 17th of April, 1992, would you usually have partaken in the whole process of the administration of graduation certificates?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. After each quarter, we would issue certificates about the term success of each student. At that time, on the 16th of April, we were supposed to issue these term -- end-of-term results. So in that way, we would verify that 75 per cent of the curriculum had been carried out. The meetings were already held, so we only needed to write the end-of-term certificates, based on those meetings. Up to that point, everything had been all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On this point, could I ask you, were you ever formally told that you were no longer required to continue your work as a teacher at the school?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive any official information about whether I was still employed or not. However, on that occasion, I wanted to pick up my work papers because I wanted to, in a way, provide information that I was no longer informed -- that I was no longer employed. But in a way, I was told that I really shouldn't do anything like that. I didn't receive any kind of official notification, so that there is no paper trail indicating that I had ever worked at that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you speak of that occasion, do you mean your visit to the secondary school at the end of May?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I wanted to use that visit to put that question, and this is what I did. But I didn't manage to get an answer, and I didn't manage to get my employment card which had the record of my prior employment at that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So do I take it you wanted to be told officially if you had been fired but show that you -- what happened, and up to that date you had worked in the school? That's the sort of information about your status you were looking for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that because you were working, you had your own bank account. Did your salary continue to reach your bank account after the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to that bank any more, so I don't know if my salary continued to be deposited. But I didn't receive any notification later about the amount that was on my checking account, or if there was anything on my checking account.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And can I confirm, you said you didn't go to that bank any more, but you did try to go to the bank once after the 17th of April, did you?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I said yesterday, that at one time I tried to go to the bank and that I got an answer that without a decision by the Crisis Staff, I could not get a hold of money from that account. And this was after the 22nd of April. I don't remember if it was perhaps the beginning of May, but it was definitely after my husband had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And also for the record, was it the normal practice that you would receive notification that your salary had been put into your account?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school took care of these administrative questions, so that -- the institution where I worked. So I didn't receive anything informing me about my salary, not -- up until the 16th of April. And then after that, I didn't go there any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I wonder whether you can seek from the witness any information as to whether since the end of the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether she has tried to get the balance out of her account in that bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, I think Her Honour's question is quite clear. Have you tried to access the account that you had in Bosanski Samac since you left and particularly since the end of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the end of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and I was absent the entire time, absent from Bosnia and Herzegovina -- I didn't have any contact with Bosanski Samac at all. I wasn't able to go to Bosanski Samac at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So since you left Bosanski Samac in September 1992, you haven't been back to Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you have known -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, I was just wondering whether you had tried by way of a telephone call to the bank or whether by way of writing a letter to the bank from wherever you were living, to again see what the balance was and to close the account and get that balance remitted to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't do that. I didn't even try.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Delic, before the break, you were describing to us how you had -- at least on one occasion yourself, seen women who were going out to do labour tasks, being put onto -- being picked up by a truck. And I understood you to say that the women who were being put on the trucks were women who were, prior to the war, had worked maybe as clerks or worked in shops and that, and then in that period after the takeover, that they would be made to go to the fields and do labour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you did also mention in your evidence that at that period that many of the Serb women and children had been moved out of the area for their own safety. And I'd just like to ask you some questions on that evidence. When you say "at that period," could you indicate which period you're talking about, which month you mean, that this occurred.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This occurred already in the month of March 1992, perhaps even at the end of February, March, April, until the middle of May or the end of May, when the new authorities realised that life can be normalised in these new conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you said that Serb families or women and children had been moved out for their own safety, do you mean that they had been forced to move out or there had -- you had witnessed families moving out of the town?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were leaving, according to their own free will, their own personal wish, using vehicles which they had. And they went with children and came back, perhaps, when they wanted -- once they felt the situation was improved or better. In any case, there was no ban or movement or any kind of order that they had to leave or come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I clarify? Although you've said that some of the Serb women and children had left the town in April -- or on the 17th of April, 1992, and immediately after that, you did still have Serb neighbours who were living in and around your apartment or house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So you then -- I believe you testified that many of the non-Serb women, some of them who you'd seen get onto the truck, had previously worked in shops or as clerks. And I understood you to say that afterwards, that the positions they had held were filled by people of Serb ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that in those shops, the non-Serb saleswomen -- besides the non-Serb saleswomen, there were also Serb saleswomen who continued to carry out their duties while these other non-Serb women were -- lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So do I understand that earlier when you spoke about the authorities harmonising or normalising conditions of life, you meant insofar as the -- those of Serb ethnicity could continue working in their jobs and continue their lives?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, do you think you could ask the witness to answer your question, page 40, lines 3 and 4, as to the position -- to use your words, "the positions they had held, were they filled by people of Serb ethnicity," please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Delic, do you have any knowledge of situations where there were jobs previously held by a non-Serb that after the 17th of April, they were replaced by someone of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say it more clearly. For example, if we're talking about a supermarket which at that point employed only non-Serbs, because all the others were absent. Once they came back, the women or the saleswomen who were not Serbs lost their jobs, and these others could continue working in their posts. They were used in a way at that time, because there was nobody there to do this work. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you explain for us -- when you say "at that time" -- "they were used at that time, because there was nobody to do this work," what time period do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am thinking of the period from the end of April until May. Middle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry. So you mean that the Serb women were used to do the work because there was no non-Serb -- no non-Serb people there to do the work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were carrying out that job because they had come back from their exile, and they continued to work in their former jobs, while the others, the non-Serb workers -- women, were prevented from continuing to carry out their jobs. They lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you witnessed some of those Serb women who had lost their jobs being put onto trucks and taken to do farm labour; is that correct? Some of those non-Serb women who had lost their jobs being put onto trucks and taken to do farm labour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge about whether or not the women put on the trucks received any payment for the work that they carried out?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't receive any payment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And do you know this from speaking to them, or are you -- do you have another reason why you say that they didn't receive payment?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this because I had conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know if any of the Serb women who were working in other sorts of work, so non-farm labour, received payment for the work they carried out?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably received payment for the work that they were carrying out in their regular jobs. Yes, this is something that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can I just clarify. You say you know it, but you've also said that they probably received it. Is this something that you believe they received, or again, you know it because of a specific source of information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I lived in a street where they continued to live -- Serb women continued to live, in conversations with them, they explained that they worked at Tekstilac, a factory for ready-made clothing. That's where they were sewing uniforms, and that they received salaries for their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've explained your knowledge of any of the work that women did after the 17th of April. And I know that your own husband was detained. Were any of your male relatives or male non-Serb neighbours also required to do work?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband's brother will over the next few months, in the period from the summer, July, August, and so on, until the month of November, be carrying out forced labour of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you say "of that kind." What exactly -- what were the tasks that he was required to do?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would go to the fields. They would go to places where the front lines were quite close. And that's where they would dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think the transcript -- if you look at line 19 of page 42, you'll see that -- this is an obvious error. The witness would appear to be saying that her husband's brother will be doing forced labour over the next number of months. I think we should --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Amend that, clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Again, Mrs. Delic, on the record it's showing that your testimony is that your brother-in-law will be performing this kind of labour in the months to come in the future. Could you just please clarify for the record when exactly you meant that he was required to carry out these tasks?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on such work obligation for the months of July, August, September, and so on, until the month of November, when he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This was 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your brother-in-law receive any payment, to the best of your knowledge, for the digging of trenches that he carried out?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never received any payment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you have some contact with your brother-in-law during this period so he could tell you this directly?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have contact with him, with him and his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did he tell you specifically that he hadn't been paid or that he received no payment for the tasks?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about it. And in any event, he did say that they didn't receive any kind of compensation for that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And your brother-in-law is a Muslim as well, like your husband?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you said he was arrested in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You testified earlier this afternoon that, up until the 27th of June, no one had ever approached you about being required to go out on some form of labour. Can you please tell us what happened on the 27th of June to change that. Did someone come and ask you to join any of these work forces?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZANA DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of June, a soldier came into the courtyard of my house, a soldier by the name of Stojan Blagojevic. His intention was to tell my neighbour downstairs that he had been receiving greetings from her husband from Orasje, from across the Sava River, on a daily basis, because the husband of that woman had joined the Croatian army, or the HVO, or whatever.
